# How the Forge Works

This is the plain-English guide. No jargon. If you only read one page, read this one.

This is also what Bakunawa teaches from. It ships inside the app rather than being fetched, so what
he tells you always matches the version you are actually running — and this page is generated from
that same text, so the app and the website say the same thing by construction.

---

## What Siklab does

You describe an app you want. A team of AI workers builds it, tests it in a real browser, and hands
you a working app plus a short guide on how to use it.

You do not write code. You do not manage the team. You say what you want, answer a few questions,
and approve the design.

---

## The five workers

Each owns one job and hands to the next. That separation is the whole point: **the worker that
builds is not the worker that checks.**

- **Mayari** reads your idea and works out what you actually meant — the screens, the data, the
  behaviour. She asks questions. That is not stalling; a brief that is wrong in scope produces an
  app that is wrong everywhere.
- **Tala** draws a real, clickable mockup. **You approve it before any code is written.** This is
  the cheapest moment in the whole process to change your mind, and it exists so that you can.
- **Apolaki** writes the actual application against the mockup you approved.
- **Sidapa** opens the finished app in a real browser and clicks through it. When something fails he
  says so, and the work goes back for repair rather than forward to you.
- **Yagu** packages it and hands it over with an account of what was checked.

Three others appear less often: **Bakunawa** (chief of staff — ask him when you are stuck),
**Bathala** (escalation), and **Indianale** (architecture).

---

## Where you are in control

Four points are yours, and the product will not move past them without you:

1. **The brief** — nothing starts until you say what you want.
2. **The scope** — Mayari confirms her understanding before design begins.
3. **The design** — nothing is built until you approve a mockup.
4. **The finish** — you decide whether it is good enough, and you can send it back.

---

## If something's wrong

Tell Mayari in plain words: *"the total is wrong when I delete a row"*, or *"I want a monthly
view"*. She sends it back to be fixed and returns with a new version. You do not need to know
whether that counts as a bug or a new feature — just say what's wrong.

**If a build stalls or stops repeatedly, it is usually the AI engine, not Siklab.** Some CLIs throw
provider errors far more often than others. If it keeps happening, switch to **claude** or **codex**
in Settings → Engines and try again.

**Ask Bakunawa** — bottom right of the app. He knows this page, the current product facts, and where
your work is. Start there.

**Report a problem** from the top bar when something is genuinely broken. It attaches your version,
your OS and an optional screenshot. **Do not put API keys, passwords or customer data in a report** —
it is not automatically redacted.

**Forgot your password?** `cd ~/.siklab-core && ./siklab-api-<platform> recover` prints a one-time
key, valid 15 minutes.

---

## Finding things later

- **Start** — begin something new
- **Sessions** — every build you've run; open one to see its history and its app
- **Attention** — things waiting on a decision from you. It should be empty most of the time; if
  something's there, it genuinely needs you
- **Files** — every app and guide you've been given, ready to download
- **Settings** — connect your AI, set your password, check for updates, enter a licence

Your work is on disk, in ordinary folders you can open in any editor:

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| Projects and generated apps | `~/.siklab/workspaces/` |
| Mockups and delivered artefacts | `~/.siklab/vault/studio/` |
| The application itself | `~/.siklab-core/` |

Nothing is locked, encrypted, or in a proprietary format.

---

## What "tested" actually means

When Mayari says a requirement was **checked**, Sidapa opened the app in a real browser and tried
that exact thing. There's a saved record of it.

When she says something **couldn't be confirmed**, the test didn't complete. That is not the same as
"it's broken" — it means nobody verified it, so treat it as unknown and try it yourself.

**Checked is not the same as correct.** Verification covers the flows it was asked to cover. It is
not proof the app has no bugs, and it is not a security review.

---

## What happens to your data

This is easy to overstate, so here it is plainly.

**Siklab runs on your machine.** There is no Siklab server holding your projects. Your work, your
database and your credential key live in `~/.siklab`, readable only by your account.

**But "runs on your machine" is not "nothing ever leaves your machine".** Four things do:

- **Your brief and code go to your AI provider.** Siklab has no AI model and no API key of its own —
  it drives the CLI *you* installed and signed in to. That exchange is between you and them, under
  your agreement with them. We never see the content or your credentials. **This is how the product
  works and there is no version of it that doesn't.**
- **Update checks** ask whether a newer version exists.
- **Problem reports**, only when you choose to send one.
- **Licence activation and renewal** are recorded.

There is **no product analytics and no telemetry**. Your source, prompts, project content and
generated output are never collected.

---

## What you own

**You own what the factory produces for you. You do not own the factory.**

Everything Siklab builds for you — source, assets, documentation, including anything built during
the trial — is yours. Use it, change it, host it, **sell it**. No royalty, no attribution, and none
of our code is inside it.

Siklab Core itself is licensed to you, not sold. Run it, yes; redistribute, resell, host it as a
service, or extract its agents and prompts, no.

One honest caveat: generated projects usually pull in third-party libraries under their own
licences. We cannot grant rights we do not have — check them before shipping commercially.

---

## The trial, and what happens after

The trial gives you **everything** — no restricted features, no project limit, no card, no account.

**The clock starts on your first build**, not when you download or install. Set up today, start
properly next week if you like.

When it ends, **nothing is taken away.** Everything you built stays on your machine and stays
openable, runnable and exportable. A plan is needed only to *start* something new.

---

## What Siklab does not do

- It does **not** deploy or host your applications.
- It does **not** include an AI subscription — you bring your own CLI or key.
- It does **not** guarantee generated code is correct, secure, or ready to ship.

Anyone claiming an AI tool produces guaranteed production-ready software is selling something.
Siklab tells you what it checked and what it didn't, and the rest is your call.
